1
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
The New York City Police Department (NYPD) is
the largest municipal police department in the United
States, with approximately 35,000 officers and 15,000
civilian employees , and is responsible for protecting
the safety of New York City’s 8.5 million residents and
tens of millions of annual visitors. Although New York
City remains the nation’s safest big city, with shooting
incidents at historic lows, gun violence is a persistent
problem. As part of its decades -long effort to combat
the scourge of gun violence and protect both the public
and police officers in the line of duty, the City has
banned assault weapons since 1991—a policy the
NYPD supported 35 years ago and continues to support today.
The NYPD respect s individuals’ Second Amendment rights. Those rights may be fully honored while
also prohibiting individuals from possessing assault
weapons, as both New York State and New York City
currently do. As respondents explain, assault weapons
create extraordinary risks for the safety of police officers and pose significant operational challenges for law
enforcement (see Cook County Br. 31 -36; Connecticut
Br. 31-32). The NYPD’s experience confirms that the
proliferation of such lethal weapons on the streets of
New York City would put officers at heightened risk of
death or injury , raise the stakes in the already tense
and tactically complex situations to which they must

2
respond, and ultimately frustrate the Department’s efforts to protect public safety.
This Court has long recognized “the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” Dist rict of Columb ia v. Heller, 554
U.S. 570, 627 (2008) (citing 4 Blackstone 148 –149
(1769)). The NYPD offers this brief to provide a law -
enforcement perspective on why the weapons at issue
in these cases are distinctively dangerous and to urge
the Court to uphold the challenged statutes.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The NYPD’s  experience confirms  that assault
weapons, carried legally or illegally, pose a unique and
particularly significant threat to police officers and to
the NYPD’s mission . Most directly, because assault
weapons are far more powerful and deadly than handguns, police officers are increasingly likely to die or be
seriously injured in the event that it becomes legal,
and thus more common , for those weapons to be possessed and carried in New York City . NYPD officers
respond to thousands of calls related to guns every
year and spontaneously encounter people bearing
handguns as well. If the NYPD’s experience stands for
anything, it is that officers are always at  some risk
when interacting with individuals who are armed. The
legalized ownership and carrying of assault weapons
on New York City’s streets would dramatically increase that risk.

3
Less directly, but perhaps more fundamentally, if
assault weapons become legal to possess and carry in
New York City, the Department’s task of maintaining
order and protecting the public will become much more
difficult and frau ght. If New York City residents and
visitors are publicly carrying assault weapons, the
NYPD ultimately may have to similarly arm some significant portion of its officer ranks to ensure that they
are not outgunned in the event of a shootout . Making
assault weapons anything close to standard issue
would change the nature of policing, for the worse. Assault weapons cannot be holstered in the manner of a
handgun, meaning that an officer holding an assault
weapon has fewer options when reacting to an unpredictable situation, limiting their ability to use less  lethal force options . More generally, an officer holding
such a weapon becomes less approachable and more
militarized in the eyes of our community partners ,
eroding the trust that the NYPD needs to effectively
do its job.
Finally, since assault weapons can only be carried
openly, officers who see a person bearing such a
weapon in New York’s crowded public spaces will be
placed in a near-impossible dilemma, with potentially
life-or-death consequences, between intrusive investigation and respect for civil liberties. T he Constitution
was not meant to place law-enforcement officers in this
type of no-win position with lives at stake. States and

4
local jurisdictions should have discretion, consistent
with the Second Amendment, to decide that the concerns expressed here require prohibiting assault weapons within their borders.
ARGUMENT
A. Assault weapons create extraordinary
risks for the safety of police officers.
Policing is difficult and often dangerous work anywhere, but the risks to officer safety are heightened in
a large city like New York. New York is a city of sidewalks, parks, and public transit. Many, if not most, police interactions occur in the  City’s crowded public
spaces. While state law bars firearm possession in certain identified “sensitive location[s],” see N.Y. Penal
Law § 265.01-e, those account for just a portion of the
City’s roadways, sidewalks, and buildings.  In an era
when many residents may  carry concealed handguns
legally, NYPD officers have learned through training
and experience how to manage their encounters with
individuals carrying handguns and how to protect
themselves and the public in those situations. But
widespread public access t o assault weapons would
change this risk calculus dramatically . Because assault weapons  have the  ability to rapidly fire many
rounds of ammunition at extremely high velocity, they
pose an exceptionally high risk to officer safety as compared to other firearms. Put simply, in the NYPD’s experience, assault weapons are “dangerous and unusual

5
weapons” in the context of the practical and life -ordeath considerations involving officer safety.
1. Assault weapons, such as the AR -15, are high -
powered semiautomatic firearms originally designed
for military use (see JA55-56). They can load and discharge ammunition rounds at rapid speed—much
faster than manually operated firearms.  Detachable
magazines allow a shooter to reload rapidly and potentially discharge hundreds of rounds in quick succession. Assault weapons are also incredibly powerful.
Each round from an assault weapon has up to four
times the muzzle velocity of a handgun round, making
them significantly more accurate from long range .1
When used by experienced shooters, or with the addition of certain accessories, the capabilities of assault
weapons approach those of machine guns. See Garland
v. Cargill, 602 U.S. 406, 411 (2024).
Because of their rapid rate of fire , quick reload
time, high muzzle velocity, and accuracy, assault
weapons are uniquely lethal.  As compared to a handgun, “[t]he higher speed of a bullet from an AR -15
causes far more damage after it hits the body and

1 See Peter M. Rhee et al., Gunshot Wounds: A Review of
Ballistics, Bullets, Weapons, and Myths, 6 J. Trauma Acute Care
Surg. 80, 853–67, 859 (June 2016); JA19.

6
drastically reduces a person’s chances of survival.”2 Indeed, the AR -15 fires bullets at such a high velocity
“that it can eviscerate multiple people in seconds.” 3
The NYPD is well aware of research showing that
shootings where assault weapons were used resulted
in an average of 2.3 times more people killed and 22.7
times more people wounded compared to incidents
with other types of guns.4
2. The capabilities of assault weapons present
acute risks for police officers in the line of duty. Although shootings are at historic lows in New York City,
NYPD officers still routinely respond to reports of incidents involving guns. In 2024 alone, officers  responded to 73,588 calls related to weapons —an average of more than 200 calls per day —and made more
than 4,000 gun arrests. 5 That is on top of the thousands of daily interactions that officers have with
members of the public through routine investigative
encounters, vehicle stops, and other calls for service,

2 N. Kirkpatrick, Atthar Mirza &  Manuel Canales, The Blast
Effect, Wash. Post (Mar 27, 2023),
https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/interactive/2023/ar-15-
damage-to-human-body.
3 Id.
4 See Everytown for Gun Safety, Mass Shootings in the United
States (March 2023), https://perma.cc/44AH-K8ZF.
5 NYPD Use of Force Report at 18 (2024), https://perma.cc/RY5L-
5NVF.

7
where officers have no advance knowledge about
whether a firearm may be present.
These situations are often fraught and volatile.
Whether an officer is responding to an interpersonal
dispute, a person experiencing a mental -health crisis,
or an active crime, the presence of a firearm heightens
the risks for both the officer and the public. Officers
are trained in how to handle these tense and potentially dangerous situations, including through the use
of verbal commands, de-escalation tactics, and, if necessary, the use of force. Nevertheless, encounters with
individuals in possession of firearms can  have devastating consequences  for officers: Between 2000 and
2024, 19 members of the NYPD were  shot and killed
in the line of duty, and 119 officers were shot and injured.6
The proliferation of assault weapons on the streets
of New York City  would put police officers at even
greater risk of death or serious bodily injury. Given the
uniquely lethal nature of assault weapons and their
ability to inflict damage faster and at a larger scale
than other types of firearms , their legalization would
almost certainly lead to more police officers being shot
and killed in the line of duty. Each interaction with a
person carrying an assault weapon would pose the risk

6 Id. at 72.

8
of more bullets being fired in rapid succession, from
longer range, and each bullet would be significantly
more likely to kill a responding officer.
Although the NYPD ensures officers have access to
high-quality firearms and protective equipment while
on duty, widespread civilian access to assault weapons
would leave officers outgunned and underprotected.
Most officers are issued a 9-millimeter semiautomatic
handgun, with capabilities inferior to that of an assault weapon. Only a small percentage of officers assigned to specialized units, such as the Emergency
Services Unit , are authorized to carry an assault
weapon or equivalent type of firearm. And although
the standard bullet-resistant vests available to NYPD
officers are effective against 9 -millimeter handguns,
they are not equipped to stop bullets fired from an assault weapon. As discussed more below, the likely result is that the NYPD will need to take steps to arm
more of its officers with high-powered assault weapons
and heavy vests with ballistic plates—a costly and difficult decision that would involve significant operational challenges.
3. The dangers that assault weapons pose to police
officers are not merely theoretical. Already, one out of
every five law -enforcement officers killed by a gun is
killed by an assault weapon. 7 One such tragedy

7 Brady United Against Gun Violence, Assault Weapons and High
Capacity Magazines, https://perma.cc/N7KG-LP4Q.

9
occurred in New York City in July 2025, when a man
carrying an assault weapon walked into the lobby of a
Midtown Manhattan office building and opened fire. In
a matter of minutes, the gunman shot and killed four
people, including Officer Didarul Islam, a three -year
veteran of the NYPD who was working a security detail in the building. Notably, the gunman had legally
purchased the weapon from his supervisor at work,
who had previously acquired the gun lawfully  out of
state.8 This accords with national data showing that a
significant portion of guns used in crimes were purchased legally.9
Law-enforcement officers across the country have
experienced similar tragedies attributable to  assault
weapons. For example, in Charlotte, N.C., four police
officers were killed and four more were injured while
trying to serve warrants at a residence, after a man
opened fire on them from a second-floor window using

8 See Pooja Salhotra, Gunman’s Mental Health History Did Not
Prohibit Gun Purchase , N.Y. Times (July 29, 2025),
https://perma.cc/VW4Y-9TUU; Mahsa Saeidi, Authorities
Investigating if Gunman in NYC Office Shooting Legally
Purchased Rifle from Boss, CBS News (July 31, 2025),
https://perma.cc/6TN7-7792.
9 Meg Anderson, Thousands of Guns Are Found at C rime Scenes.
What Do They Tell Us?, NPR (Dec. 17, 2025),
https://perma.cc/V8Z2-GWGN.

10
an assault weapon.10 In Detroit, an officer responding
to a 911 call about a weapon was shot and killed by a
man firing an assault weapon from an apartment
building.11 And in Philadelphia, six officers were
wounded by gunfire from an assault weapon during an
hours-long standoff in which a man fired over 100
rounds at them before surrendering.12
In short, the unusually dangerous nature of assault
weapons means that legalizing their possession and
carry would create grave and unprecedented risks to
the safety of police officers, in ways that the current
laws allowing handgun possession and carry do not.
B. Legalizing assault weapon s would
create significant operational
challenges for the NYPD and other lawenforcement agencies charged with
protecting public safety in urban areas.
A ruling for petitioners would also lead to difficultto-navigate operational challenges for the NYPD and

10 Kevin Shalvey & Meredith Deliso, AR-15 Rifle Recovered from
Scene Where 4 Law Enforcement Officers Killed in Charlotte:
Police, ABC News (Apr. 30, 2024), https://perma.cc/Y4JW-WHSG.
11 Assoc. Press, Detroit Police Officer Killed After Confronting
Man with Assault -Style Weapon  (July 7, 2022),
https://perma.cc/QD38-LMYQ.
12 David Chang, Brian Sheehan & Siobhan McGirl, Man
Sentenced to 120-240 Years in Prison for Shooting Philly Officers,
NBC10 Philadelphia (July 10, 2025), https://perma.cc/F972 -
5AX5.

11
for similarly situated public -safety agencies.  The
NYPD’s mission is to “ enhance the quality of life in
New York City” by, among other things, enforcing the
law, protecting the people of the City, and maintaining
order.13 Through experience, the NYPD has learned
that it cannot achieve its mission when those it is
charged with protecting —law abiding citizens or otherwise—carry firearms that are significantly more capable of harm than what regular NYPD officers carry.
The legalization of assault weapons in New York City
would have the practical effect of forcing the NYPD to
consider similarly arm ing its regular -duty officers .
This arms race would reduce public safety, change the
very nature of policework in the City , and create an
intimidating barrier to community engagement. Further, NYPD officers would be placed in a terrible bind,
caught between respecting the rights of those bearing
firearms openly—assault weapons can be carried in no
other way—and their sworn duty to protect the public
from harm.
1. NYPD officers interact with the public at a volume that is unmatched in any other American city. 14
And because of New York City’s population density,

13 NYPD Patrol Guide, Proc. No. 200 -02 (Oct. 24, 2025),
https://perma.cc/Q4CB-JACY.
14 See NYPD Use of Force Report at 18 (noting that NYPD officers
responded to nearly seven million 911 calls in 2024).

12
those interactions often occur in  bustling public
spaces. An officer can rarely predict when a call for assistance or other encounter will turn from benign and
peaceful to volatile and dangerous.  Through training
and accountability, the NYPD has dra matically reduced firearm discharges by its officers over the past
five decades.15 Nonetheless, the NYPD has long recognized that its officers cannot achieve their protective
goals if the weapons they carry place them at a disadvantage relative to the people they are responsible for
keeping safe, law-abiders and law-breakers alike.
History provides pertinent examples of the NYPD’s
need to remain on equal footing with the arms-bearing
individuals that officers encounter. In 198 6, 22-yearold Officer Scott Gadell was killed during a shootout
with a person armed with a semiautomatic handgun,
while Gadell was in the cumbersome process of reloading his .38 -caliber six -shot revolver . The NYPD  responded by transitioning its force to “speed loaders,” in
the hope that it would prevent officers from being
placed at a similar disadvantage again.16

15 Id. at 15.
16 See NYPD, Fallen Finest, Police Officer Scott A . Gadell,
https://perma.cc/CL4Y-G2E4; Chels ia Rose Marcius, Queens
Ceremony Honors Memory of NYPD’s Scott Gadell, Slain While
Reloading Low-Capacity Weapon in 1986, N.Y. Daily News (June
29, 2016), https://perma.cc/R2HK-6TQF.

13
Later, in the 1990s, the NYPD recognized that officers were “increasingly outgunned” in encounters involving firearms, and the Department transitioned its
service weapon from the  .38-caliber revolver to the
quicker-to-reload and more powerful 9 -millimeter
semiautomatic handgun, capable of carrying 10
rounds.17 The NYPD made this transition with significant reservations about whether the  new firearms
were too powerful  and dangerous  to be used  in the
crowded New York City landscape .18 Ultimately, the
Department determined that it could not send its officers to work in an environment where their service firearm provided insufficient protection for themselves
and the public.
A ruling that makes it impossible to ban  assault
weapons in New York City would leave regular-duty
NYPD officers even more outgunned than they were in
the 1990s. If history is any indication, s uch a change
would likely result in the NYPD considering  steps to
arm more and more officers  with a weapon that
matches the firepower of the armed individuals that
they are bound to encounter  on the City’s sidewalks
and roadways . While the NYPD’s leadership had

17 Craig Wolff, New York City Police to Replace Revolvers w ith
Semiautomatics, N.Y. Times  (Aug. 21, 1993),
https://perma.cc/JT66-7L4K.
18 See id.

14
reservations about transitioning to a more- powerful
service handgun in the 1990s, arming a large portion
of the NYPD’s force with assault weapons involves
risks and consequences far more significant than what
the NYPD faced then. The NYPD may nonetheless be
forced to accept these risks and consequences when officer safety is at issue.
2. Equipment changes that better protect officers
from the dangers of assault weapons would have repercussions on policing. An officer’s day-to-day work is
significantly altered, and in many situations undermined, when they are carrying an assault weapon and
wearing a bulky vest with ballistic plates. Unlike
handguns, a ssault weapons are large  firearms that
cannot be carried hands -free on an NYPD duty belt.
Holding such a weapon while engaged in a street patrol or in any interaction with the public makes an officer less agile and  less able to respond in situations
that are often unpredictable, as does wearing a plated
vest. And if an officer is already holding a firearm, using a less lethal form of force becomes more difficult .
The NYPD requires officers to holster their firearm “as
soon as practicable.”19 But assault weapons can never
be put away.
Relatedly, because an assault  weapon cannot be
holstered out of sight in the manner of a handgun, the

19 NYPD Patrol Guide, Proc. No. 221 -01 at 3 (July 10, 2025),
https://perma.cc/RT9J-YPN4.

15
officer’s weapon would also likely become a focal point
of any community interaction. This would present a serious impediment to the NYPD’s work. Community engagement is a crucial part of effective policing , which
is why the Department’s mission statement specifies
that officers work “in partnership with the community” to achieve the NYPD’s goals. 20 It barely needs
saying that an officer carrying an assault weapon and
wearing plated body armor in a public space is not presenting a face of community partnership. The NYPD’s
most basic mission includes “reduc[ing] fear .”21
Achieving that mission becomes much more difficult
when rank -and-file officers look less like crime -
fighting partners and more like soldiers sent to neutralize an enemy force.
3. The legal possession and carrying of assault
weapons in New York City’s crowded public spaces
would also force officers to make rapid, highly fraught
determinations based on little information  about who
is likely to be a lawful and peaceful firearm carrier and
who intends to use the firearm for criminal harm. To
be sure, police officers are tasked everyday with decisions that test the tensions between public safety and
constitutional rights. Officers rely on their training,

20 NYPD Patrol Guide, Proc. No. 200 -02 (Oct. 24, 2025),
https://perma.cc/Q4CB-JACY.
21 Id.

16
understanding of the law, and best judgment to determine which activities require further investigation
and which do not.
But the legalization  of assault weapons  in New
York City would make these encounters even more difficult to navigate . The presence of these weapons in
public places would lead to alarm and increased emergency calls, and it would be the rare situation where
an officer could discern without intrusive investigation
whether the person was  carrying the firearm  legally.
Judging correctly whether an individual carrying an
assault weapon means no harm could be the difference
between life and death . NYPD officers, committed to
following the law and keeping people safe, would regularly be put in a seemingly impossible position. A constitutional doctrine that puts our officers in this bind
ignores the reality of policing in a densely populated
and pedestrian-focused city like New York.
NYPD officers regularly do not encounter this problem with handgun possession because the City’s licensing regulations allow only concealed carry. See 38
R.C.N.Y. § 5-01(b). Currently, if an officer sees a firearm carried in the open or receives a report of such behavior, there is probable cause to believe that a violation has occurred, permitt ing the officer to intercede .
That certainty would disappear if the carrying of assault weapons became legal because assault weapons
can only be carried openly.  NYPD officers should not
be placed in a position where they are constantly

17
having to determin e, with no good options,  how to
thread the needle between Second Amendment rights
and their mission to protect the public from harm.
4. Finally, the NYPD is aware that organizations
representing other law-enforcement entities have filed
a brief in support of petitioners, arguing, among other
things, that those entities “welcome the help” from citizens armed with assault weapons “in fighting crime”
so that the “burden on law enforcement” is eased. 22
The NYPD strongly disagrees with this sentiment. I n
the NYPD’s institutional experience, the job of law enforcement will become much more difficult and dangerous, at least in a densely populated city such as
New York, if members of the public are carrying highly
powerful and particularly lethal firearms.
Whatever the merits of these amici’s views when it
comes to their own jurisdictions, they simply make no
sense in a place like New York City. The Second
Amendment should pose no barrier to New York City
and New York State choosing a different path for protecting our officers and the public.


22 Brief of Amici Curiae National Sheriffs’ Association and
Western States Sheriffs’ Association in Support of Petitioners, at
16-17.

18
CONCLUSION
This Court should affirm the decisions of the courts
of appeals.
